implementation_notes: Rust inverts the classic split: the lock does not sit beside the data, it owns the data - Mutex<T> has a type parameter representing the data it protects, and the data can only be reached through the RAII guards returned by lock()/try_lock(), which release on drop and therefore remove the classic 'forgot to unlock' failure (panics excepted; a panic while holding the lock poisons it). What remains of the pattern is publication: a shared lockable object is handed out as Arc<Mutex<T>>, the guard doubles as the mutex lock and as the capability to mutate, and the type system refuses both unsynchronised access and copies of a lock. Poisoning turns a panicking lock holder into a recoverable error on the next lock() call, and the std mutex is not reentrant, so recursive APIs must be restructured around unlocked helpers.
pitfalls: std::sync::Mutex is not reentrant: locking the same mutex twice on one thread deadlocks; expose unlocked internal helpers instead of calling public locking methods while a guard is held.
Poisoning is advisory but pervasive: lock() returns a Result, and unwrapping or ignoring a PoisonError hides the fact that a previous holder panicked mid-invariant.
Never hold a std guard across .await: it blocks the executor thread and usually makes the future non-Send; async code needs tokio::sync::Mutex or a design that releases before awaiting.

Arc<Mutex<T>> shares one lock, but nothing prevents the same lock from being reached through two guards (lock order inversions between objects), and Mutex<RwLock<T>>-style layering multiplies the discipline - keep one lock per invariant.
